title: A NaN or Inf training loss makes JSONEncoder throw, so /complete is never sent and the task is orphaned.
scenario:
1. A federated round is started with learning_rate=0.05. The server accepts up to 1e-1 (federated.py:164).
2. The loss diverges, so the LoRATrain .train callback reports NaN losses.
3. Outcome.trainLoss is the mean of the last 5 losses, which is NaN (FederatedTrainer.swift:172). runTrain sets metrics["final_loss"]=NaN (NodeService.swift:386) after the adapter has already been uploaded.
4. FleetClient.complete calls `JSONEncoder().encode(body)`. The default nonConformingFloatEncodingStrategy is .throw, so encoding throws EncodingError.invalidValue before any request goes out.
5. execute() only records lastError 'Couldn't report ...' and returns to polling.
6. The server task stays 'running' with an online owner. The previous finding explains why sweep and cancel never free it. The round never aggregates and the requester's long-poll never sees a terminal status.
A val_loss of NaN or Inf (NodeService.swift:387) triggers the same failure.
evidence:
FleetClient.swift:161 `let metrics: [String: Double]` and :166 `try await send("POST", "tasks/\(taskID)/complete", json: try JSONEncoder().encode(body))` use a default JSONEncoder, which throws on non-finite Doubles.
NodeService.swift:386-387 `if let l = outcome.trainLoss { metrics["final_loss"] = l }` / `val_loss` has no isFinite check.
fix: Drop non-finite metrics before encoding (`metrics.filter { $0.value.isFinite }`), or set `encoder.nonConformingFloatEncodingStrategy = .convertToString(...)`. Also report a NaN loss as status 'failed' so a poisoned adapter doesn't enter FedAvg.

UPHELD(high): I could not refute the claim. Every step checks out at origin/ios-node, and the server part checks out at origin/fleet.

1. FleetClient.swift: `complete()` builds a `Body` with `metrics: [String: Double]` and encodes it with `try JSONEncoder().encode(body)`. The encoder is a default one and never sets nonConformingFloatEncodingStrategy. Foundation's default strategy is .throw, so a NaN or ±Inf value anywhere in the metrics dictionary throws EncodingError.invalidValue. That happens inside the `json:` argument, before `send` builds or sends any request.
2. FederatedTrainer.swift:146 appends every `.train` loss with no finiteness check. Lines 170-172 average the last 5 losses (`tail.reduce(0,+)/Float(tail.count)`), so a single NaN or Inf in the tail makes trainLoss non-finite. validationLoss is passed through unchecked.
3. NodeService.swift:386-387 copies both values into metrics with no isFinite guard. Line 388 returns status "succeeded".
4. NodeService.execute (about lines 213-226) calls `client.complete` once inside a detached Task. Any error is caught and turned into `lastError = "Couldn't report ..."`. Nothing retries, and nothing falls back to sending a sanitized result.
5. Server side, fleet.py:132-142 `sweep()` only requeues tasks whose `assigned_to` node is not `_online`. The node keeps heartbeating and polling, so it stays online and the task stays 'running' forever. `cancel()` (fleet.py:280-289) only sets `cancel_requested` on a running task. The node has already finished, so it never reads the flag, and nothing moves the task to a terminal state.
6. The trigger is reachable. federated.py accepts learning_rate up to 1e-1, which goes to Adam(learningRate: 0.1). Adam at that rate on LoRA can plausibly diverge to NaN or Inf, and a float16 overflow could do the same.

The round therefore never gets this node's completion and never aggregates, and the requester never sees a terminal status. Medium severity is fair. The adapter is uploaded before the failure, but no completion arrives to account for it. | fix: In NodeService.runTrain, check `outcome.trainLoss` and `outcome.validationLoss` with `isFinite`. If either is non-finite, return `.failure("training diverged (non-finite loss)")` so the poisoned adapter never enters FedAvg. As a fallback, filter metrics in FleetClient.complete with `result.metrics.filter { $0.value.isFinite }`. You could also use an encoder with `nonConformingFloatEncodingStrategy = .convertToString(positiveInfinity: "inf", negativeInfinity: "-inf", nan: "nan")`, but the Python side would then receive strings. Separately, when `complete` fails on a non-network error, have execute() retry once with a `.failure(...)` result so the task always reaches a terminal state.

title: Pausing the node (background or Serve off) reports the in-flight task as terminal 'failed' instead of releasing it, which defeats the server's requeue.
scenario:
1. An iPad is training its shard of a federated round, or running an untargeted generate task.
2. The user switches apps for a few seconds. scenePhaseChanged(.background) cancels the loop.
3. The training callback sees Task.isCancelled and stops, or the generate stream throws.
4. execute() builds `.failure("node paused ...")`, and inside the background grace it POSTs /complete with status 'failed'.
5. The server treats 'failed' as terminal. It never calls _requeue_or_lose, so the task is not retried on this node when it comes back, or on another node for generate.
6. The round aggregates without this iPad's contribution, or fails outright with 'no node produced an adapter' if it was the only trainer.
The code comment assumes this is the same as the server's 75 s requeue, but it is not. Going offline gets a retry (attempts < 2); a brief pause gets a permanent failure.
evidence:
NodeService.swift:12-14: 'A task in flight at that moment is reported as failed (the worker would otherwise requeue it after 75 s anyway).'
NodeService.swift:202-203 `} else if Task.isCancelled { result = .failure("node paused (app backgrounded or serving turned off)")`, followed by complete() at :214-216.
fleet.py:266-277: complete accepts 'failed' and calls `_finish(task, status, ...)`, which is terminal. Only sweep/_load reach `_requeue_or_lose`.
fix: Add a release outcome to the protocol, for example status 'requeue' that maps to _requeue_or_lose. Alternatively, have the client skip /complete when it pauses and let the sweep requeue the task.

title: Task completion is POSTed once and never retried, so the task stays 'running' forever and its federated round never aggregates
scenario: The iPad finishes a train_lora task, or reports 'node paused' during the background grace window. The single POST /tasks/{id}/complete then fails: the grace expires and the app is suspended mid-request, Tailscale blips, the worker returns a 5xx, or the 45 s timeout hits. The error only goes into lastError. When the app comes back, the node heartbeats and long-polls again, so the worker always sees it as online. The worker's sweep only requeues tasks whose node is offline, and next_task never revisits the node's old assignment. So the task stays 'running' and assigned to this iPad forever. FederatedRounds._maybe_aggregate waits until every round task is terminal, so the round never aggregates and the requester waits forever. I confirmed this by running a copy of fleet.py outside the repo: claim a task, post one event, never complete, keep polling past offline_after, call sweep. Result: 'task status after polling past offline_after: running assigned_to ipad-abcd1234'.
evidence: NodeService.swift:214-226: `let reported = await Task.detached { do { try await client.complete(...); return nil } catch { return error.localizedDescription } }.value ... if let reported { lastError = "Couldn't report \(taskID): \(reported)" }` (no retry, nothing persisted). fleet.py:135-137 sweep: `stale = [t ... if t.meta["status"] in ("assigned", "running") and not self._online(self.nodes.get(t.meta.get("assigned_to")...))]`. fleet.py:198 next_task refreshes `last_seen` on every poll. federated.py:210: `if any(t is None or t.meta["status"] not in TASK_TERMINAL for t in tasks): return`.
fix: Persist the pending (taskID, result) and retry complete with backoff until it gets a 2xx, 409 or 404, including after a pause/resume. Also make the worker requeue or lose tasks still assigned to a node when that node asks for its next task.

1. **The iPad reports once and gives up.** In origin/ios-node NodeService.swift `execute()` (around lines 210-226), `client.complete` is called exactly once inside `Task.detached`. On error the message only goes into `lastError`, then `currentTask = nil` and the loop goes back to `nextTask`. Nothing is persisted or retried. FleetClient.swift `complete` calls `send` directly, with no retry and a 45 s request timeout.

2. **A lost completion is never recovered while the node stays online.**
   - In origin/fleet worker/fleet.py, `sweep()` only picks up assigned or running tasks whose node fails `_online` (no `last_seen` within `offline_after`, 75 s).
   - `next_task` sets `nodes[node_id]["last_seen"] = now()` on every loop pass.
   - `_claim` only looks at `status == "queued"` tasks and never revisits the node's old assignment. `next_task` just overwrites `current_task`.
   - `heartbeat` and `node_events` also refresh `last_seen`.
   
   So a node that keeps long-polling (every 25 s) never goes offline, and its orphaned task stays assigned or running forever.

3. **Cancelling does not help.** `cancel()` on a non-queued task only sets `cancel_requested`. The task reaches a terminal state only through `complete()` from the owning node or through `sweep` when the node is offline. Neither happens here.

4. **The round never aggregates.** In federated.py, `_maybe_aggregate` returns early if any round task is not in `TASK_TERMINAL`, so that round hangs.

**Trigger:** any one-off failure of the single POST while the app stays up is enough: a worker 5xx, a timeout, or a dropped connection where the request never reached the worker. The background-suspension variant only applies when the suspension is shorter than about 75 s. Longer suspensions make the node go offline and `sweep` requeues the task, so that part of the scenario is narrower than claimed. The foreground failure modes alone still confirm the defect. Severity is high for federated rounds (a permanent hang with no way out through cancel) and medium for single generate tasks. | fix: **Client (NodeService.execute):**
- Keep the (taskID, result) pair in a pending-report slot, persisted to UserDefaults or disk so it survives a pause or relaunch.
- Retry `complete` with backoff until the worker answers 2xx, 409 or 404. Do this before claiming new work, and again on resume.

**Worker (fleet.py next_task):**
- Before calling `_claim`, look for tasks still assigned or running on this node_id (except one the node is legitimately still working on).
- Pass any such task to `_requeue_or_lose`, or to `_finish(..., "cancelled")` if `cancel_requested` is set. Since the node only polls when it is idle, any older assignment is orphaned.
- Optionally, make `cancel()` of an assigned or running task finish it right away after a grace period.

title: Overwriting backgroundGrace on a quick background, foreground, background sequence leaks a UIBackgroundTask, and iOS terminates the app
scenario: The node is serving with a task in flight. The app goes to background: backgroundGrace = id1, stop(), and grace Task G1 awaits the old loop l1 (draining pump events and `client.complete` over the network). Before l1 finishes, the user returns (.active calls resumeIfEnabled, which starts a new loop l2) and backgrounds again: `guard loop != nil` passes and `backgroundGrace = beginBackgroundTask(...)` overwrites id1 with id2. When l1 finishes, G1 calls endBackgroundGrace(), which ends id2 (the wrong one). G2 then finds .invalid. id1 is never ended, and its own expiration handler also calls endBackgroundGrace(), which sees .invalid and returns. iOS kills the app when id1's background time expires.
evidence: Lines 82-91: `guard loop != nil else { return }; backgroundGrace = UIApplication.shared.beginBackgroundTask(withName: "node-pause") { [weak self] in Task { @MainActor in self?.endBackgroundGrace() } }; let l = loop; stop(...); Task { @MainActor in await l?.value; self.endBackgroundGrace() }`. Lines 98-101: endBackgroundGrace ends whatever identifier is currently stored. The expiration handler also ends the task asynchronously instead of inside the handler.
fix: Capture the identifier locally (`let id = UIApplication.shared.beginBackgroundTask { UIApplication.shared.endBackgroundTask(id) }`). End that exact id both in the expiration handler (synchronously) and after `await l?.value`. Use a set or array if several grace periods can overlap.
verifier_notes: UPHELD(medium): I re-read origin/ios-node:ios/AgentConsole/Node/NodeService.swift and the sequence works as claimed. In `scenePhaseChanged(.background)` (lines 81-92), `stop()` sets `loop = nil` straight away, but the old loop task l1 keeps running after cancel. Inside `execute`, l1 still awaits `GPUGate.release`, `buffer.finish` plus `await pump.value` (detached, posting events over the network) and then `client.complete` in a fresh detached Task (lines 208-221). So l1 can take several seconds after cancel, and longer if the network is slow. If the app becomes .active during that time, `resumeIfEnabled` calls `start()`, which passes `guard loop == nil` and creates l2. A second .background then passes `guard loop != nil` and line 84 overwrites `backgroundGrace` (id1) with id2. The single stored identifier is the only record of id1, and `endBackgroundGrace` (lines 98-102) ends whatever is stored at that moment. So when l1 finishes, G1 ends id2 early, and G2 later sees `.invalid`. id1's expiration handler hops to the main actor, sees `.invalid` and returns without ending id1. iOS kills apps whose background task is still running when its time expires, so the leak can get the app killed in the background. The timing window is narrow (the user has to foreground and background again while l1 is still finishing its network calls), so low severity is right. The fix captures each identifier locally and ends that exact id, both on completion and synchronously in the expiration handler. | fix: In the .background case: `var id: UIBackgroundTaskIdentifier = .invalid; id = UIApplication.shared.beginBackgroundTask(withName: "node-pause") { UIApplication.shared.endBackgroundTask(id); id = .invalid }` (or keep a Set<UIBackgroundTaskIdentifier> on the main actor). After `await l?.value`, end only that captured id, and only if it hasn't been ended already, then remove it from the set. Do not store a single shared `backgroundGrace`.

UPHELD(high): I could not refute the claim. On origin/ios-node, ios/AgentConsole/Node/NodeService.swift keeps a single stored `backgroundGrace` (line 54). Every `.background` transition with a live loop writes a new identifier into it at line 84 without checking for one already there. `endBackgroundGrace()` (lines 98-102) ends whatever identifier is stored at that moment. Nothing else guards this: AgentConsoleApp.swift:43-49 forwards every scenePhase change to `scenePhaseChanged`, and `.active` calls `resumeIfEnabled()`, which calls `start()`. `start()` creates a new loop l2 as soon as `loop` is nil, and `stop()` already set it to nil. So on the second background, `guard loop != nil` passes and id1 is overwritten by id2.

The old loop l1 can easily outlive a quick app switch:
- With a task in flight, `execute` waits for the generation or training to unwind. Cancellation is only checked between chunks, after `convo.send` or at `try Task.checkCancellation()`.
- It then waits for `GPUGate.release`, the pump drain (`await pump.value`) and a detached `client.complete` network call (lines 208-221). These are deliberately detached, so they are not cancelled.
- A train_lora task can take much longer.

Meanwhile l2 is usually cancelled quickly, because its URLSession long-poll is cancellation-aware. The two grace Tasks then call `endBackgroundGrace()` in either order. Whichever runs first ends id2, and the second sees `.invalid`. id1 is never ended. When id1's time runs out, its expiration handler calls `endBackgroundGrace()`, which also sees `.invalid` and returns. Per UIKit's documented contract, an app that fails to end a background task before it expires is terminated.

The sequence needs background, then foreground, then background again while a task is still being reported. That is plausible but narrow, and the result is a background termination rather than data loss, so low severity is right. Separately, the expiration handler ends the task in a hopped `Task { @MainActor }` rather than synchronously inside the handler. That is a minor additional weakness. | fix: In scenePhaseChanged(.background), capture the identifier locally. Do not use the single stored property. Example:

var id: UIBackgroundTaskIdentifier = .invalid
id = UIApplication.shared.beginBackgroundTask(withName: "node-pause") {
    if id != .invalid { UIApplication.shared.endBackgroundTask(id); id = .invalid }
}
let l = loop
stop(status: "Paused (app in background)")
Task { @MainActor in
    await l?.value
    if id != .invalid { UIApplication.shared.endBackgroundTask(id); id = .invalid }
}

In practice, hold `id` in a small @MainActor final class box, or a per-call Set<UIBackgroundTaskIdentifier>, so the expiration handler and the completion path share it safely. Each grace period then ends exactly its own task, and the expiration handler ends it synchronously. Drop `backgroundGrace` and `endBackgroundGrace()`, or keep them only as a set of outstanding IDs.

UPHELD(medium): I could not refute this. I traced the code on origin/ios-node, ios/AgentConsole/Node/NodeService.swift lines 77-101.

1. First background: `loop` is l1, which is in the middle of execute(), so `guard loop != nil` passes. `backgroundGrace = id1`. stop() cancels l1 and sets `loop = nil`. Grace task G1 waits on `await l1.value`.
2. Can l1 still be running a few seconds later? Yes, it can. After cancellation, execute() still runs `buffer.finish()`, then `await pump.value`, which drains events through `client.postEvents` over the network. It then waits on `client.complete` in a detached task, which cancellation does not stop and which uses URLSession's default timeout of up to 60 s. A train_lora task may also notice cancellation late. So l1 can easily outlive a quick trip through the app switcher.
3. The user comes back: `.active` calls resumeIfEnabled(), then start(). `loop == nil`, so l2 starts while l1 is still finishing.
4. Second background: `loop` is l2, so the guard passes again. `backgroundGrace` is set to id2 and id1 is lost, because no other copy of it is kept. stop() cancels l2. Grace task G2 waits on l2, which stops quickly because cancelling it interrupts the nextTask long-poll.
5. Whichever of G1 and G2 finishes first calls endBackgroundGrace(). That ends id2, the only id still stored, and sets the field to `.invalid`. The other call sees `.invalid` and returns.
6. Nothing ever calls endBackgroundTask(id1). When id1's time runs out, its expiration handler runs `Task { @MainActor in self?.endBackgroundGrace() }`, which sees `.invalid` and does nothing. Apple's documentation says that failing to end a background task before its time expires causes the system to kill the app. That is the termination the claim describes.

Severity stays low. The node was already paused, and the worker requeues an unreported task after 75 s. The effect is a watchdog kill and crash report while the app is in the background, and possibly a lost failure report. No user data is lost.

A minor point: in the single-background case, ending the task from a Task scheduled inside the expiration handler, rather than synchronously in the handler, is fragile but usually works. The defect that actually causes the kill is the overwritten id. | fix: Keep each grace id in its own local variable and end exactly that id once, on whichever path gets there first. For example: `var id: UIBackgroundTaskIdentifier = .invalid; id = UIApplication.shared.beginBackgroundTask(withName: "node-pause") { UIApplication.shared.endBackgroundTask(id); id = .invalid }`, or hold a Set<UIBackgroundTaskIdentifier> on the main actor that can be removed from in a way that is safe to call twice. After `await l?.value`, end that same captured id if it has not already ended. Never end the id held in the shared `backgroundGrace` field. The expiration handler must call endBackgroundTask synchronously, not through a new Task.
